title: Colour, Contrast, and Redundant Cues

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Colour, Contrast, and Redundant Cues.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Colour is powerful because the visual system notices contrast and change quickly. But colour is contextual, not a reliable channel that carries a fixed meaning by itself. The ability to distinguish two colours depends on their lightness, saturation, size, separation, surroundings, display, and viewing conditions.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Small pale marks and thin text are particularly difficult to discriminate.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Why does that happen?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Design therefore begins with the meaning that must be perceived, not with a preferred palette. If a state means “requires action,” ask how that meaning survives when colour is unavailable, indistinct, or misunderstood. Pair colour with a label, icon, shape, pattern, position, status text, or changed control state.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use contrast to establish hierarchy and legibility; do not assume contrast alone establishes a relationship or consequence.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: This matters beyond accessibility. A dashboard that makes an outlier legible through colour plus a direct label is faster for everyone to scan. A form error marked with red plus a useful message gives people a diagnosis and recovery route. A selected navigation item that changes colour, weight, position, and state is easier to verify at a glance.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Do not turn this into “never use red and green.” The lesson is to treat colour as one signal in a deliberately redundant system. Also distinguish visual contrast from semantic contrast: a bright destructive button may be easy to see but still be ambiguous about what it destroys. The visual signal and the language must agree.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at visual comparison: when colour disappears?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Imagine one compact chart shown twice. Version A distinguishes three categories only with nearly identical thin hues and a tiny legend. Version B uses a high-contrast palette, direct labels, line patterns, and a clearly marked outlier. Remove colour from both: only the second preserves category and outlier information. Redundancy is what makes the visual robust.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at mechanism and boundaries?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Colour perception depends on relationships, not isolated hex values. Apparent colour changes with surrounding colour, luminance, display, ambient light, viewing angle, and the size of the mark. Thin strokes and small text offer less signal than large regions.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Different colour-vision capabilities alter which hues can be discriminated, while ageing, glare, fatigue, and low-quality displays can reduce contrast for anyone.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Separate three jobs. Legibility needs sufficient contrast between foreground and background. Differentiation needs categories that can be told apart. Meaning needs an understandable mapping from appearance to state or action.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Passing a text contrast check does not prove that two chart series are distinguishable; distinguishable hues do not explain which series requires action; a red button does not explain what it will delete.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Design redundancy at the semantic layer. Pair colour with labels, position, shape, pattern, line style, iconography, and programmatic state as appropriate. Do not merely add an icon whose meaning also depends on colour. In charts, direct labels often reduce legend search. In forms, an error summary plus field-level message supports both discovery and correction.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: For focus, selection, hover, visited, disabled, loading, warning, success, and failure, document the non-colour evidence.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Test in the component's real size and state, under zoom and reflow, with forced or high-contrast settings where relevant. Grayscale is a useful challenge but not a complete accessibility test. The goal is not a colourless interface; it is meaning that remains available when the colour channel weakens or disappears.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Treat colour as a governed semantic channel
turns.text: What changes when we look at treat colour as a governed semantic channel?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Contrast is checked across component states, not just static text: placeholder, disabled, focus, hover, error, selected, charts, overlays, and text on imagery. Tokens document intended combinations and prohibit unsafe pairings, while real pages test effects of opacity, layering, and adjacent colours.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Meeting a numeric threshold does not prove that dense or tiny content is readable.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Audit colour in states, not only in style guides. Ask what happens to loading, selected, disabled, warning, success, error, visited, and data-series states when someone cannot distinguish a hue, uses high zoom, sees the product outdoors, or consumes a screenshot in grayscale.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: <! -- Editorial: manual revision; curated product example --

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Illustrative scenario: a train-platform alert. The platform changes from 4 to 7. Red text alone can be missed or misread. Place the new platform in the journey, pair colour with words and an icon, maintain contrast, and expose the update to assistive technology. Test whether travellers can identify the right platform under time pressure.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How does this connect to what we have already learned?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: lesson 8 explained that visual structure guides grouping; lesson 9 explained that attention is limited. This lesson makes one constraint concrete: salient colour is not automatically understandable colour. lesson 100 carries the same reasoning into reading, type, and scan paths.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Take a screenshot of a product with a status, chart, form error, or selected control. Temporarily remove colour mentally or with a grayscale filter. List every meaning that vanishes, then add the smallest second cue that restores it.
